A practical guide to how to introduce a new dog to your home, with low-stress management, reward-based training, common mistakes, body-language clues, and signs that veterinary or behavior help is appropriate.

Quick Answer

Dogs may bark excessively because of alarm, excitement, frustration, fear, attention seeking, boredom, or separation-related distress. The useful first step is identifying exactly what predicts the barking; the solution for a dog barking at passersby is different from the solution for a dog panicking when left alone.

Map the Barking Before Trying to Stop It

For several days, note where the dog is, what appears immediately before the barking, how long it lasts, and what ends it. Door sounds, windows, other dogs, departures, play, confinement, and requests for attention create very different behavior patterns.

Reduce Rehearsal of Predictable Triggers

Block a busy window, add distance from dogs on walks, use gates during deliveries, or change the setup so the dog is not practicing the same high-intensity response dozens of times a day.

Teach a Specific Alternative

Choose a behavior that can replace barking in that situation: going to a mat when the door sounds, checking in with you outdoors, or settling with enrichment during quiet periods. Reward the alternative before barking escalates.

Do Not Reward Demand Barking Accidentally

If barking consistently makes a person throw a toy, open a door, or deliver attention, it can become efficient communication. Meet genuine needs, then reinforce a quieter request instead.

Fear and Alarm Barking Need Distance

A frightened dog is not simply being disobedient. Increase distance from the trigger, avoid forced greetings, and pair manageable exposure with something the dog values.

When Barking Happens Only During Absence

Vocalizing with pacing, drooling, destruction near exits, toileting, or escape attempts can indicate separation-related distress. Record a short safe video after departure and discuss significant distress with a veterinarian or qualified behavior professional.

When Barking Needs Professional Help

Sudden new vocalization can accompany pain or illness. Veterinary assessment is appropriate for abrupt behavior change or physical signs; growling, lunging, bite risk, severe fear, or separation panic also warrants qualified behavior support.

Bottom Line

Dogs may bark excessively because of alarm, excitement, frustration, fear, attention seeking, boredom, or separation-related distress. The useful first step is identifying exactly what predicts the barking; the solution for a dog barking at passersby is different from the solution for a dog panicking when left alone.

A practical guide to how to introduce two dogs safely, with low-stress management, reward-based training, common mistakes, body-language clues, and signs that veterinary or behavior help is appropriate.

Quick Answer

Growling is communication, not a diagnosis and not automatically a sign that a dog is 'dominant.' It can warn that a dog is frightened, guarding something, in pain, uncomfortable with handling, or wants more distance. Punishing the warning can make future behavior harder to predict.

Treat the Growl as Information

Stop advancing the interaction and identify what was happening immediately beforehand. A growl around food, during grooming, when approached on a bed, or when a painful body part is touched points to different underlying problems.

Create Distance Without Confrontation

Avoid looming, grabbing collars, cornering, or forcing contact. Calmly increase space and use barriers or management when needed, especially around children or visitors.

Look for Earlier Body-Language Signals

Freezing, turning the head away, lip licking, a hard stare, tucked posture, whale eye, or moving away may occur before a growl. Responding to these earlier signals can prevent escalation.

Resource Guarding Requires Management

If growling occurs around food, toys, resting places, or stolen objects, do not repeatedly take items to 'prove' control. Prevent unsafe access and use structured reward-based training.

Handling Growls May Signal Pain

A dog that suddenly growls when lifted, touched, groomed, or moved may be protecting a painful area. New handling sensitivity deserves veterinary evaluation.

Do Not Punish the Warning

Scolding, hitting, alpha rolls, or other intimidation can increase fear and may suppress the growl without removing the reason for aggression.

Get Help Before a Bite

Previous bites, snapping, escalating intensity, unpredictable triggers, or risk to children require secure management and individualized professional guidance.

A practical guide to how to introduce a dog to a cat, with low-stress management, reward-based training, common mistakes, body-language clues, and signs that veterinary or behavior help is appropriate.

Quick Answer

Chasing the tail can be brief play or excitement, especially in young dogs, but frequent or difficult-to-interrupt spinning can also reflect itch, pain near the tail or rear end, anxiety, or repetitive behavior. Frequency and the dog's ability to disengage matter.

Occasional Play Can Be Normal

A brief tail chase during playful arousal that stops easily and does not injure the dog is different from prolonged spinning or biting at the tail.

Check the Tail, Skin, and Rear End

Look for fleas, redness, wounds, hair loss, swelling, discharge, or persistent licking. Anal-area discomfort or skin disease can redirect attention toward the tail.

Track Excitement and Stress

Some dogs chase their tails during high arousal, frustration, or conflict. Note whether visitors, confinement, play, or other predictable situations precede episodes.

Interrupt With a Calm Alternative

Before the behavior escalates, redirect to sniffing, a simple cue, a food-search activity, or another low-arousal behavior. Avoid chasing or laughing if attention appears to reinforce the spinning.

Protect Against Self-Injury

Repeated biting can damage the tail quickly. Use safe management and veterinary advice rather than allowing the behavior to continue until wounds develop.

When Repetition Becomes Concerning

Episodes that are frequent, prolonged, difficult to interrupt, or interfere with eating, sleep, walking, or social interaction deserve professional assessment.

Rule Out Medical Causes First

Pain, itch, neurologic disease, and other physical problems can resemble a purely behavioral habit. A sudden onset or accompanying physical signs should be evaluated by a veterinarian.

Quick Answer

Dogs lick people for several possible reasons: social interaction, attention, interesting tastes or smells, learned reinforcement, excitement, or self-soothing. The context matters more than the lick itself, and most ordinary social licking does not need to be 'corrected.'

Social Contact and Greeting

Some dogs include licking in friendly greetings or close contact. Loose posture, voluntary approach, and easy disengagement support a social explanation.

Attention Can Reinforce Licking

Talking, laughing, petting, or pushing the dog away can all provide interaction. If licking reliably produces attention, it may become a learned request.

Skin Tastes and Smells Interesting

Salt, lotions, food residue, and unfamiliar scents can make human skin attractive. Prevent access to products that are unsafe if ingested.

Excitement and Arousal

Greeting or play can increase licking temporarily. Teaching a calm alternative such as sitting or settling can make greetings easier without punishing the dog.

Stress-Related Licking

Repeated licking in tense situations can sometimes function as a displacement or self-soothing behavior. Look at the dog's entire posture and whether the dog can move away.

Set Boundaries Consistently

If you do not want licking, calmly remove access and reward another behavior. Mixed responses—sometimes encouraging it and sometimes scolding—make the rule unclear.

When Licking Is Excessive

A sudden major increase, compulsive repetition, licking paired with nausea signs, or persistent licking of the dog's own body may require veterinary or behavior assessment.

Quick Answer

Howling can be normal communication, a response to sirens or other dogs, a way to seek social contact, or part of distress when alone. Identify whether the dog is relaxed and responsive or showing panic, pain, or another physical change.

Sound-Triggered Howling

Sirens, music, instruments, and other dogs can trigger vocal responses. This is often brief and ends when the sound disappears.

Social Contact

Some dogs howl when separated from family members or when trying to locate them. The surrounding body language distinguishes ordinary contact calling from severe distress.

Learned Attention Seeking

If howling reliably brings a person into the room or starts an activity, the behavior may be reinforced. Meet legitimate needs while rewarding quieter ways of requesting interaction.

Separation-Related Distress

Howling after departures together with pacing, drooling, destruction, toileting, or escape attempts can indicate a welfare problem rather than simple boredom.

Breed and Individual Differences

Some dogs are naturally more vocal than others. Baseline matters: a sudden change in a normally quiet dog deserves more attention than a stable lifelong pattern.

Do Not Punish Distress Vocalization

Intimidation may increase anxiety and does not teach a distressed dog to feel safe when alone.

When a New Howl May Be Medical

Pain, cognitive change in older dogs, sensory decline, or other illness can alter vocalization. Sudden or nighttime howling with physical or cognitive changes deserves veterinary discussion.

content:
A practical guide to why does my dog dig, with low-stress management, reward-based training, common mistakes, body-language clues, and signs that veterinary or behavior help is appropriate.

Quick Answer

Digging is a normal canine behavior that can be driven by scent, prey, cooling, hiding items, escape attempts, boredom, or simple enjoyment. Management works best when it targets the actual reason and, when appropriate, gives the dog a legal place to dig.

Digging for Scents or Small Animals

Concentrated digging near roots, fences, or animal tunnels can be driven by odor or prey movement. Blocking access and managing wildlife attractants may matter more than obedience cues.

Cooling Off

Some dogs scrape away warm topsoil to reach cooler earth and lie in the depression. Provide shade, water, and a cooler resting area, especially in hot weather.

Burying Food or Valued Items

Dogs may cache chews, toys, or food for later. If this is harmless, management may simply mean controlling what can be taken outdoors.

Escape Digging at Fences

Digging concentrated along a boundary is a safety problem. Supervise outdoor time, secure the perimeter appropriately, and address whatever is attracting or frightening the dog beyond the fence.

Boredom and Under-Stimulation

A dog left in a yard with little social contact or enrichment may discover that digging is highly rewarding. Add sniffing, training, play, food-search activities, and appropriate exercise.

Create a Designated Digging Area

For dogs that genuinely enjoy digging, a sandbox or loose-soil area can provide an acceptable outlet. Bury safe toys or treats there and reward choosing that location.

Avoid Punishment After the Hole Is Found

Delayed punishment cannot explain which past action was wrong. Prevent access, redirect in real time, and change the environment so success is easier.

Quick Answer

Mounting or humping can occur during excitement, play, stress, social interaction, or sexual behavior; it is not automatically about dominance. Manage the context, interrupt before arousal peaks, and check for medical irritation when the behavior appears suddenly or includes excessive genital licking.

Excitement and Overarousal

Mounting often appears during energetic play, greetings, or crowded social situations. Short breaks and calmer activities can prevent escalation.

Play Behavior

Some dogs mount during play without a sexual motivation. Watch whether both dogs remain loose and willing; intervene if the recipient avoids, freezes, growls, or tries to escape.

Stress or Conflict

A dog may mount when unsure how to respond to social pressure. Increasing space and reducing stimulation can be more useful than punishment.

Sexual Motivation

Hormones can contribute, particularly in intact animals, but neutering does not guarantee that an established learned behavior will disappear.

Learned Attention

Human reactions can accidentally make mounting rewarding. Calm interruption and reinforcement of another behavior are clearer than shouting or physical confrontation.

Medical Irritation

Urinary, genital, skin, or anal-area discomfort can increase licking or mounting. Sudden onset with discharge, frequent urination, pain, or persistent licking needs veterinary assessment.

Prevent Social Conflict

Do not let mounting continue until another dog has to defend itself. Interrupt early and give both dogs space.

A practical guide to why does my dog follow me everywhere, with low-stress management, reward-based training, common mistakes, body-language clues, and signs that veterinary or behavior help is appropriate.

Quick Answer

A dog may roll in smelly material because strong odors are intrinsically interesting, because rolling is self-rewarding, or because the scent itself becomes part of exploration. Prevention and a strong recall are usually more practical than punishment after the dog has already rolled.

Odor Exploration

Dogs experience the environment primarily through scent, and substances humans find disgusting can be highly interesting to them.

The Behavior Can Reward Itself

Rolling provides immediate sensory stimulation, so it does not require human attention to become a strong habit.

Wild-Canid Explanations Are Uncertain

Ideas about masking scent or carrying information are often proposed, but a pet dog's individual motivation cannot be determined from the behavior alone.

Prevent Access in High-Risk Areas

Scan ahead on walks, use a leash or long line where carcasses, feces, or other material is common, and keep waste cleaned up at home.

Teach an Emergency Turn-Away

Practice a cheerful recall or turn cue around low-level distractions first, then reward heavily for leaving interesting smells before the dog reaches them.

After the Dog Rolls

Avoid chasing if that turns the event into a game. Secure the dog calmly and clean the coat with a dog-appropriate product, taking extra care if the substance may be toxic or irritating.

When the Substance Could Be Hazardous

Unknown chemicals, dead wildlife, toxic algae, pesticides, or other hazardous material can require veterinary or poison-control advice, particularly if the dog licked or swallowed it.

Quick Answer

Eating grass is common in dogs and does not automatically mean illness. Some dogs appear to enjoy the texture or forage normally, while nausea or gastrointestinal discomfort may contribute in others. Frequency, vomiting, appetite, stool, and exposure to chemicals are the important clues.

Normal Foraging

Many healthy dogs occasionally eat grass and continue eating, playing, and passing normal stool. An isolated episode without illness is often not alarming.

Taste and Texture

Fresh vegetation can simply be interesting to chew. Preference for particular grass or locations may support ordinary exploratory behavior.

Nausea or Gastrointestinal Discomfort

Some dogs seek grass around episodes of nausea, but grass eating itself cannot diagnose stomach disease. Repeated vomiting, appetite loss, diarrhea, pain, or weight loss changes the picture.

Dietary Explanations Are Not Simple

Grass eating should not automatically be interpreted as a specific nutrient deficiency. Persistent dietary concerns are better addressed by reviewing the complete diet with a veterinarian.

Pesticides and Other Hazards

Do not allow grazing on recently treated lawns or plants that may be toxic. Grass containing feces, parasites, sharp seeds, or chemicals adds risks unrelated to the behavior itself.

When to Redirect

Interrupt grazing when the location is unsafe or the dog is consuming large amounts. Offer appropriate enrichment rather than punishing ordinary sniffing and foraging.

When Grass Eating Needs Veterinary Attention

Repeated vomiting, inability to keep water down, abdominal pain or swelling, blood, marked lethargy, appetite loss, or suspected toxin or foreign-body ingestion warrants veterinary care.

A practical guide to why does my dog lick me so much, with low-stress management, reward-based training, common mistakes, body-language clues, and signs that veterinary or behavior help is appropriate.

Quick Answer

Dogs eat poop (coprophagia) for several reasons, including scavenging opportunity, learned habit, competition, or attraction to undigested material. The priority is preventing access and ruling out medical problems when the behavior is new, intense, or accompanied by weight loss, diarrhea, excessive hunger, or other changes.

Scavenging Opportunity

Feces are biologically interesting to many dogs. Immediate cleanup is often the most effective first intervention because it prevents the behavior from being repeatedly rewarded.

A Learned Habit

If a dog repeatedly has access to stool, eating it can become a well-practiced routine. Prevention plus rewarding the dog for moving away from feces is more useful than punishment.

Competition or Rapid Cleanup

In multi-dog environments, competition or excitement around elimination areas may contribute. Supervise toileting and remove stool promptly.

Diet and Digestion Questions

Coprophagia does not automatically prove a vitamin deficiency. When it appears with poor body condition, diarrhea, excessive hunger, or weight loss, veterinary assessment can investigate digestion, parasites, diet, or other disease.

Stress and Environment

Confinement, inadequate sanitation, or stressful living conditions can influence some cases. Improving routine, enrichment, exercise, and cleanliness may help.

Teach Leave-It Away From Feces First

Build a reward-based leave-it skill with ordinary low-value objects before expecting success around stool. Outdoors, use a leash while the skill is developing.

Avoid Punishment Around Toileting

Scolding a dog for eliminating or approaching stool can create anxiety or encourage secretive behavior. Calm prevention and reinforcement are clearer and safer.
